title: Sum and Difference Formulas
short: sin(a + b) = sin a cos b + cos a sin b.
trouble: Students write sin(a + b) = sin a + sin b.

blocks.html: Is $\sin(\alpha + \beta)$ the same as $\sin\alpha + \sin\beta$? Try $\alpha = \beta = 45^\circ$: the left side is $\sin 90^\circ = 1$, but the right side is $\sqrt{2}$. So trig functions do not distribute over sums, and we need the real rule. It comes from distances on the unit circle.

Put $A = (\cos\alpha, \sin\alpha)$ and $B = (\cos\beta, \sin\beta)$ on the unit circle. By the distance formula, $$AB^2 = (\cos\alpha - \cos\beta)^2 + (\sin\alpha - \sin\beta)^2 = 2 - 2(\cos\alpha\cos\beta + \sin\alpha\sin\beta).$$
Now rotate the picture by $-\beta$. Distances do not change, and the points become $(\cos(\alpha - \beta), \sin(\alpha - \beta))$ and $(1, 0)$, whose squared distance is $2 - 2\cos(\alpha - \beta)$. Setting the two equal gives $\cos(\alpha - \beta) = \cos\alpha\cos\beta + \sin\alpha\sin\beta$. Replacing $\beta$ with $-\beta$ gives the sum formula, and using $\sin\theta = \cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - \theta\right)$ gives the sine formulas. Dividing the sine formula by the cosine formula gives tangent.

blocks.cap: $f(x) = \sin(x + a)$ against $g(x) = \sin x + \sin a$. They only agree when $a = 0$.

blocks.title: Without knowing the angles
blocks.q: $\sin\alpha = \frac{3}{5}$ and $\cos\beta = \frac{5}{13}$, both angles in Quadrant I. Find $\sin(\alpha + \beta)$.
steps: Fill in the missing values with the Pythagorean identity: $\cos\alpha = \frac{4}{5}$, $\sin\beta = \frac{12}{13}$.

blocks.html: Writing $\sin(\alpha + \beta) = \sin\alpha + \sin\beta$. Test with $\alpha = \beta = 45^\circ$: $\sin 90^\circ = 1$, but $\sin 45^\circ + \sin 45^\circ \approx 1.41$. Also watch the sign in the cosine formula: the sum has a minus, $\cos(\alpha + \beta) = \cos\alpha\cos\beta - \sin\alpha\sin\beta$.
